concept_edges.logic: x = y stores the value of y in x (a statement with a side effect); x == y only tests whether the two values are equal and gives a boolean. Writing = where == is meant is a compile error with int operands and a silent bug with boolean operands.
The running maximum is found by traversing the array once, keeping the largest value seen so far (starting from Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY).
i++ is shorthand for the assignment i = i + 1.
An if runs its block only when its boolean expression evaluates to true.
A comparison such as x < y produces a boolean result; comparisons together with boolean logic provide the basis for decision-making.
An if changes the default top-to-bottom flow by running a block only when its condition is true.
A data structure organizes many values of a data type; the array holds a sequence of values of one type.
Comparison operators build expressions whose value is a boolean, so one must already know what an expression is to understand a < b.
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) gives i every valid index exactly once, in increasing order.
A variable declared in the for header exists only from its declaration to the end of the for statement's block.
Valid indexes run from 0 to a.length - 1; any other index throws an exception when it is used.
A traversal uses the loop variable i as the index, so a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
The for header is exactly the three control slots, and the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
The loop update i = i + 1 comes first; ++ (and +=) are then introduced as shorthand for that update.
The init, condition and update all act on the loop variable: the init sets it, the condition tests it, the update changes it.
Control flow is the order in which statements run.
System.out.println(s); is itself a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Declaring sum inside the loop body keeps a running total across passes.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The accumulator must be declared and initialised before the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a(i) accesses element i of an array.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Array elements are accessed with square brackets, a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; the length is set at creation.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array can hold elements of any type.
misconceptions.correct_rule: All elements of an array have the declared element type.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you call length() instead of using the length field
misconceptions.correct_rule: An array's size is the field a.length, written without parentheses.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The first element of a is a[1].
misconceptions.correct_rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: initializer values go in [] instead of {}
misconceptions.correct_rule: Starting values go in braces, like int[] a = {v0, v1};.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array cannot have length 0.
misconceptions.correct_rule: new int[0] is a legal array of length 0.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Using an array means every cell must be scanned.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = compares two values instead of assigning
misconceptions.correct_rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Assigns a new value to a variable declared final.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A final variable cannot be reassigned after it is initialized; the compiler reports an error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: assigning a reference copies the object
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: b = a exchanges the values of a and b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression
misconceptions.correct_rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = b copies the value of a into b.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Changing the loop variable inside the body does not affect the loop condition; the loop still runs its planned number of times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition is tested with the current value of the variable, including changes made in the body.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped.
misconceptions.correct_rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you must write == true / == false to test a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes the if condition inside { } instead of ( ).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition of an if is written in parentheses.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The declaration only names the array; until new (or an initializer) creates it, using a[i] gives a 'variable might not have been initialized' compile-time error.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Leaves a traversal loop with return before every element has been processed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A result that depends on all elements is known only after the loop ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i.
misconceptions.correct_rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: X[i] names the whole array, not one element.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The array is a; a[i] is the single element at index i.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes else (x > 0) with a condition but no if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: else takes no condition; use else if (x > 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: == compares contents (the String == bug)
misconceptions.correct_rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; s.equals(t) compares the text.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: .equals() compares references, not contents
misconceptions.correct_rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes a + b = c; or 7 = a; as if = were a math equation.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The left side of an assignment must be a single variable; only the right side can be an expression.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The running maximum can always start at 0.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int), so that the first value read replaces it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A false condition with no else ends the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes for (int i = 0, i < n, i++).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update part.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The body of a for statement executes at most once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i declared in the for header can still be used after the loop has ended.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i declared in the for header exists only inside the loop, so using it after the loop does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever).
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an if body repeats while its condition holds
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Every if statement requires an else.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i++ increases i by 2.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a condition that never goes false still terminates
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b).
misconceptions.correct_rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations
misconceptions.correct_rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ...

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--).
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The for variable i is created once by the init, and the update changes that same variable on every pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The range of the loop variable limits the values that can be read or printed inside the loop.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The loop variable only counts passes; other values read or printed in the body are not bounded by it.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need ? : to do the same
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean
misconceptions.correct_rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

misconceptions.wrong_belief: In if (c) A; B; the statement B runs only when c is false.
misconceptions.correct_rule: B is not part of the if; it runs every time.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"
misconceptions.correct_rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them)
misconceptions.correct_rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable
misconceptions.correct_rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: an out-of-bounds read returns null (it throws)
misconceptions.correct_rule: Reading any index outside 0 to a.length - 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first
misconceptions.correct_rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: () are optional on a no-argument call like println
misconceptions.correct_rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: i = i++ increases i by 1.
misconceptions.correct_rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass
misconceptions.correct_rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: print and println behave the same (no newline difference)
misconceptions.correct_rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
misconceptions.correct_rule: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Ends the output with print and expects it to appear right away.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Finish a line of print calls with println; some systems hold print output until a newline is printed.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes int x = 5; ... int x = 10; to change x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A declaration gives a variable its name and type; a later change of value is an assignment statement such as x = 10;, not a second declaration.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Writes =< or => instead of <= and >=.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The operators are written <= and >=.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Puts a ; right after for (...) or while (...).
misconceptions.correct_rule: A ; right after the loop header is a null (empty) loop body, so the statements written after it are not repeated by the loop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; code without a loop runs once.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a statement runs without the ;
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each statement must end with ;, otherwise javac reports ';' expected.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Statements in a program can run in any order.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically.
misconceptions.correct_rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values.
misconceptions.correct_rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The then branch always runs.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The then branch runs only when the condition is true.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model).
misconceptions.correct_rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value
misconceptions.correct_rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: a = a + b adds the arrays element by element.
misconceptions.correct_rule: Java has no arithmetic on whole arrays; write a loop that adds a[i] + b[i] for each i.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times.
misconceptions.correct_rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count.

mis_edges.logic: With ++i in the update of for (int i = s; i < n; ++i), i is increased before the body runs, so the first pass uses s + 1.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.

mis_edges.logic: i declared in the for header can still be used after the loop has ended.
mis_edges.twin_logic: i declared in the for header exists only inside the loop, so using it after the loop does not compile.

mis_edges.logic: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

mis_edges.logic: A variable declared inside the loop body keeps its value from one pass to the next.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.

mis_edges.logic: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The for variable i is created once by the init, and the update changes that same variable on every pass.

mis_edges.logic: Changing the loop variable inside the body does not affect the loop condition; the loop still runs its planned number of times.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The condition is tested with the current value of the variable, including changes made in the body.

mis_edges.logic: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.

mis_edges.logic: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

mis_edges.logic: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

mis_edges.logic: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

mis_edges.logic: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The for variable i is created once by the init, and the update changes that same variable on every pass.

mis_edges.logic: The range of the loop variable limits the values that can be read or printed inside the loop.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The loop variable only counts passes; other values read or printed in the body are not bounded by it.

mis_edges.logic: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.

mis_edges.logic: println with nothing to print can be written System.out.println; without the parentheses.
mis_edges.twin_logic: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

mis_edges.logic: print and println do the same thing, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on separate lines.
mis_edges.twin_logic: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.

mis_edges.logic: println(s) prints a newline and then s.
mis_edges.twin_logic: println(s) prints s and then the newline.

mis_edges.logic: System.out.println("x is 5"); sets x to 5 (text inside the quotes is run as code).
mis_edges.twin_logic: Characters inside double quotes are printed literally; println only displays them and changes no variable. Only an assignment such as x = 5; sets x.

mis_edges.logic: The running maximum can always start at 0.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int), so that the first value read replaces it.

mis_edges.logic: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command.
mis_edges.twin_logic: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

mis_edges.logic: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

mis_edges.logic: Statements in a program can run in any order.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

mis_edges.logic: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line.
mis_edges.twin_logic: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.

level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: An out-of-bounds read returns null (or 0). Right rule: Reading or writing any index outside 0 to a.length - 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and returns no value.

Points to LT: the bounds check runs at every access, at run time. Inconsistent application: the trace accepts an index of a.length on the last pass (or -1 on the first) but rejects it elsewhere, or reads 'some value' there. (here mixing in: "an out-of-bounds read returns null (it throws)")

wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n, which is out of bounds for an array of length n.

Conservation: a loop bounded by i < a.length stays within bounds when the array size changes. Changing < to <= adds one pass that throws, and starting at 1 or ending at a.length-1 silently skips an element.

wrong rule: int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed. Right rule: The declaration only names the array variable; until new (or an initializer) creates the array, a[i] gives the compile-time error 'variable a might not have been initialized'.
wrong rule: An array can hold elements of any type. Right rule: Every element of an array has the declared element type: an int[] holds only int values, a String[] only String references.

wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type is the array's length. Right rule: Each bracket pair adds one dimension (int[] is 1-D, int[][] is 2-D); the length is not part of the type and is fixed only when the array is created.

Points to LT: declare, then create, then initialize, in that order. Inconsistent application: the trace treats a as already created on some lines (reading a[i] straight after 'int[] a;') while requiring new on others. (here mixing in: "int[] a; already makes an array that can be indexed")
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The name a (written a[] in the book) denotes the whole array; a[i] denotes the single element at index i.

Conservation: rewriting 'int[] a' as 'int a[]' keeps the meaning. Changing the element type changes which values may be stored and the default values. Deleting the creation step breaks the program at compile time.
wrong rule: Initializer values go in [] instead of {}. Right rule: Starting values go in braces, as in int[] a = {v0, v1};; brackets only mark the type or an index.

Points to LT: an array of length k+1 is created, then v0..vk are stored at indices 0..k in order. Inconsistent application: the trace puts the first value at index 1 for one initializer but at index 0 for another, or counts the length differently. (here mixing in: "initializer values go in [] instead of {}")

wrong rule: The number of brackets in an array type or initializer is the array's length. Right rule: Brackets give the number of dimensions; an initializer's length is the number of values between its braces.

Conservation: adding or removing a value changes the length. Code that uses a.length (e.g. rank.length) adapts, while code with a hard-coded size breaks. Reordering values changes which index holds which value.
wrong rule: a = a + b adds the arrays element by element. Right rule: Java has no arithmetic on whole arrays; write a loop that adds a[i] + b[i] for each i.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: A traversal may cover only part of the array or stop early (as in a search); indexing reaches single elements directly.

Points to LT: initialize i, test, run the body with the current i, update, test again. Inconsistent application: on some passes the update is applied before the body, or a[i] is traced with the previous i. (here mixing in: "a = a + b adds the arrays element by element")
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.
wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is used.

Conservation: running the index downward (a.length-1 to 0) visits the same set of elements in reverse order, harmless for a sum but not for a shift. Starting at 1 or stopping at a.length-1 drops an element. Invariant: before pass i, elements 0..i-1 have been processed.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, and if (!b) tests that it is false, so == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: You need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.
wrong rule: You need ? : to turn a boolean expression into a boolean (ok = x > y ? true : false). Right rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.
wrong rule: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). Right rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false, e.g. (year % 4 == 0).

Points to LT (arithmetic first, then comparisons, then !, &&, ||, left to right, with short-circuit). Applied unevenly: the student evaluates && before a comparison in one sub-expression, or evaluates the right operand of && on a pass where the left was already false. (here mixing in: "you must write == true / == false to test a boolean")

wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean, which cannot be compared with <); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a while re-tests its condition and repeats its body for as long as the condition is true.

wrong rule: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if. Right rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

Rewriting with De Morgan (!(a && b) as !a || !b) keeps the value for every input; swapping the operands of && keeps the truth value but can change whether the right operand is evaluated (and whether a guard still protects it); changing < to <= changes the result only at the boundary value.
wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: == compares the contents of two Strings. Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; "abc" == "ab" + x is false even when x is "c"; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile (use s.compareTo(t)).
wrong rule: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b). Right rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

Points to LT (evaluate both operands, promote to a common type, then compare). Applied unevenly: the student treats < as <= on the boundary pass of a loop, or compares an int with a double as ints on one line and as doubles on another. (here mixing in: "90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100")
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them and produces a boolean.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters; it is == that compares references.

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: e.g. runs a later line before an earlier one, lets an if that was already passed fire again later, or ends the program when a loop or a false if ends instead of continuing with the next statement. (here mixing in: "Statements in a program can run in any order")
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them). Right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

Reordering two statements generally changes the result whenever one reads a variable that the other writes (e.g. swapping x = x + 1 and print(x)); reordering is safe only for statements that touch disjoint variables. Moving a statement into or out of a branch or loop body changes how many times it runs (0, 1 or n).

wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
wrong rule: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression". Right rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

Points to LT (replace each variable with its current value, then apply operators in precedence order). Applied unevenly, a student substitutes current values for some variables and old or future values for others, or respects precedence in one subexpression only. (here mixing in: "a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"")
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

Adding parentheses that match the default grouping keeps the value, and rewriting with an equivalent formula (4 * (x - 3) as 4*x - 12) keeps it for ints. Changing one operand's type (3 to 3.0) can change both the result's type and its value.
wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. Right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.

wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. Right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.

wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. Right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.
wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. Right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

Applies the for sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on the first pass only, re-runs the init after a pass, or skips the test on some passes. (here mixing in: "The body of a for statement executes at most once")

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).
wrong rule: an if body repeats while its condition holds. Right rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.
wrong rule: Every if statement requires an else. Right rule: An if statement may stand alone; the else part is optional.
wrong rule: A false condition with no else ends the program. Right rule: When an if condition is false and there is no else, execution continues with the statement after the if.
wrong rule: The then branch always runs. Right rule: The then branch runs only when the condition is true.
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: In if (c) A; B; the statement B runs only when c is false. Right rule: B is not part of the if; it runs every time.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true. Right rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.

wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.

wrong rule: Whether the branch runs is decided by the condition after the branch, or from the point inside the body where the condition becomes true. Right rule: The condition is tested once, before the branch; the whole branch runs if it was true at that moment and none of it runs otherwise.

wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. Right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

Applies the if rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition on some visits but not others (e.g. runs the branch on every loop pass without testing), runs the branch after a false test, or re-checks the condition after the branch has run. (here mixing in: "an if body repeats while its condition holds")
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.
wrong rule: you need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
wrong rule: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true. Right rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.

Negating the condition swaps which inputs run the body; changing < to <= changes only the boundary value. Adding a statement under a braceless if does not put it in the body. Whatever the condition, code after the if still runs exactly once.
wrong rule: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x. Right rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
wrong rule: i++ increases i by 2. Right rule: i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.

Applies the increment rule (LT) unevenly: uses the old value in one expression and the new value in another for the same i++, or performs the increment at the end of the loop body instead of where it is written. (here mixing in: "x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x")
wrong rule: i = i++ increases i by 1. Right rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.
wrong rule: i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value. Right rule: i is a position; a[i] is the value stored at that position.
wrong rule: The first element of a is a[1]. Right rule: Numbering begins with 0; the first element is a[0].
wrong rule: new int[n] has slots 0 to n, inclusive. Right rule: The slots are 0 to n - 1.
wrong rule: a(i) accesses element i of an array. Right rule: Array elements are selected with square brackets, a[i]; a(i) would be a call of a method named a.

wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.
wrong rule: X[i] names the whole array, not one element. Right rule: The array is a (a[] in the book); a[i] is the single element at index i.
wrong rule: After i changes, X[i] still refers to the element at the old value of i. Right rule: a[i] is evaluated with the current value of i each time it is executed.

Points to LT: in a[i], a is evaluated, then i with its current value, then the bounds check, then the element is read or written. Inconsistent application: i is updated on one line, but a later a[i] is traced with the old i. (here mixing in: "i and a[i] are the same thing, so the position is the stored value")
wrong rule: Using an array means every cell must be scanned. Right rule: Arrays allow random access: a[i] reaches one element directly, and a loop visits only the elements the task needs.

Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.
wrong rule: You call length() instead of using the length field. Right rule: An array's size is the field a.length, written without parentheses; length() is a String method.

Points to LT: a.length is read every time the loop test i < a.length runs. Inconsistent application: the trace uses a.length as the last valid index on some passes (as if the test were <=). (here mixing in: "you call length() instead of using the length field")
wrong rule: An array cannot have length 0. Right rule: new int[0] is a legal array with length 0; args is such an array when no arguments are typed.

Conservation: for a given array object a.length never changes, so loops bounded by a.length stay correct when the array is created with a different size. Reassigning a to another array changes a.length.
wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. Right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.

wrong rule: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. Right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

wrong rule: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times. Right rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ...

wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. Right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones.

Applies the body rule (LT) unevenly: runs all body statements on some passes but only some on others, includes the statement after the loop on some passes, or uses stale values from the first pass later. (here mixing in: "The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start")

wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. Right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop.

wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command. Right rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. Right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. Right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

wrong rule: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does. Right rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

Moving a statement from inside the body to after the loop changes it from running once per pass to once in total (and vice versa); reordering two body statements that share a variable changes the results (e.g. increment before vs after use).
wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.

Applies the init-test-update rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on some passes, skips the test or the update on a pass, or re-runs the init. (here mixing in: "++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass")

wrong rule: a condition that never goes false still terminates. Right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.

wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.

wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. Right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

Changing < to <= adds one pass; starting at 1 instead of 0 removes one; doubling the step halves the passes; reversing init and bound with i-- visits the same values in reverse order (and still processes the same set only if both ends are adjusted).

wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is in scope only to the end of the body, so each pass declares and initializes it afresh and it does not keep the previous pass's value.

wrong rule: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update. Right rule: The for variable i is created once by the init, the update changes that same variable on every pass, and i exists only until the end of the for statement.
wrong rule: i declared in the for header can still be used after the loop has ended. Right rule: i declared in the for header exists only inside the loop, so using it after the loop does not compile.
wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

Applies the scope rule (LT) unevenly: lets a body variable keep its value from the last pass on some passes but not others, or uses the for variable after the loop in one place but not another. (here mixing in: "a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations")

Moving a declaration from before the loop into the body re-initializes the variable every pass and makes it unusable after the loop; moving a for-header declaration out (int i; for (i = 0; ...)) keeps the loop's behaviour and makes i usable after it.

wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. Right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

wrong rule: Changing the loop variable inside the body does not affect the loop condition; the loop still runs its planned number of times. Right rule: The condition is tested with the current value of the variable, including changes made in the body.

wrong rule: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does. Right rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

wrong rule: The range of the loop variable limits the values that can be read or printed inside the loop. Right rule: The loop variable only counts passes; other values read or printed in the body are not bounded by it.

Applies the init-test-update rule (LT, loop_control) unevenly to the loop variable: forgets one update, applies a different step on some passes, or re-initializes it mid-loop. (here mixing in: "The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same")

wrong rule: The for variable i is a new variable on every pass rather than one variable changed by the update. Right rule: The for variable i is created once by the init, the update changes that same variable on every pass, and i exists only until the end of the for statement.

wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. Right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.
Shifting the start and the bound by the same amount keeps the number of passes but changes the values the body sees; assigning to the loop variable inside the body changes the pass count.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.

wrong rule: The running maximum can always start at 0. Right rule: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int) so that the first value read replaces it.

Points to LT: on each pass, compare a[i] with max and assign max = a[i] only if a[i] is larger. Inconsistent application: max is overwritten without the comparison on some passes, or compared with a stale value. (here mixing in: "The running maximum can always start at 0")

Conservation: replacing > by >= keeps the maximum value but changes which tied position is the last one recorded. Remembering the index of the extreme instead of its value conserves the specification.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.
